query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-existing nanoscale elemental segregation and short-range order in as-synthesized FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles lower local melting onset temperatures, leading to earlier and heterogeneous phase transition.
generation.material_initial_state: As-synthesized FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles produced by rapid quenching, exhibiting inherent compositional modulations and short-range order.
generation.intervention: Perform a controlled post-synthesis annealing at moderate temperature (e.g., 600 °C for 1 hour) to homogenize the elemental distribution versus leaving a control sample untreated.
generation.conditions: Heating in an inert atmosphere with a standardized ramp rate (e.g., 5 K/min) up to the melting regime; nanoparticle size maintained around 5–10 nm.
generation.structural_mediator: Local compositional domains and short-range ordering that create regions with reduced cohesive energy.
generation.mechanism: Localized areas with elemental segregation exhibit a depressed melting point; as temperature increases, these regions act as nucleation sites for premelting, causing a heterogeneous phase transition across the nanoparticle.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with pronounced pre-existing segregation (unannealed) will begin to show melting features (e.g., endothermic events in DSC) approximately 50–100 K lower than homogenized (annealed) counterparts, and the melting will progress via localized regions.
generation.baseline: As-synthesized, rapidly quenched nanoparticles with inherent short-range order serving as the baseline.
generation.boundary: Valid for nanoparticle sizes around 5–10 nm and heating rates near 5 K/min under inert (Ar) atmosphere.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the melting depression may vary with the degree of segregation and may be influenced by other nanoscale effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles – one left as synthesized and one homogenized by annealing. Subject both sets to identical DSC tests and in situ TEM heating experiments to compare the onset temperature and melting progression.
measurements: In situ TEM imaging for localized melting
EDX mapping before and after heating
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the homogenized nanoparticles do not exhibit a higher melting onset temperature (with a difference near the predicted 50–100 K) or show identical melting behavior to the unannealed sample, then the role of pre-existing segregation is not significant, falsifying the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: As shown in Table S2, the thermal decomposition of the five metal salts occurs at different temperatures. Figure 3a shows the temperature profile along the depth. Once the thermal decomposition temperature (TD) of the metal precursor is reached but below the melting temperature (TM) of the corresponding metals, the thermal decomposition of the mixed metal salt particles adsorbed on the LIG occurs accompanied by gas release, and then each CrMnFeCoNi nanoparticle with homogeneous composition is generated by nucleation and growth of the species from the decomposition of each mixed metal salt particle. This particle is likely to be at the site of the original metal salt particle (the light green zone in Fig. 3a). When the temperature is above TM while below the boiling temperature (TB) of metals, the metallic elements are in the liquid phase to form molten beads. Since metals are nonwetting with carbon, these liquid metal beads tend to aggregate and grow bigger to minimize their surface energy at high temperatures. In this paper, thermal analysis of the CoCrFeMo0.85Ni HEA powder was carried out via differential thermal analysis (DTA) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to assess the thermodynamic properties of HEA, including the solidus, liquidus and phase transition temperatures. With detailed characterization of microstructures in the DTA sample, the critical temperatures determined in thermal analysis can be correlated with microstructural features to examine phase formation and formation of precursor states from compositional modulations in HEA. This will provide fundamental understanding on intermetallic strengthening mechanism and phase stability for processing of HEAs.

papers.title: Microstructure and Thermal Analysis of Metastable Intermetallic Phases in High-Entropy Alloy CoCrFeMo0.85Ni.
papers.approach: Differential thermal analysis (DTA) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) with repeated heating/cooling cycles and microstructural characterization by SEM/EDX
papers.findings: Identified distinct thermal events, including an exothermic phase transition initiating around 800 °C and endothermic dissolution around 1212 °C, with the final solidification window between ~1200 and 1320 °C. Minor elemental segregation was observed, suggesting thermally driven compositional modulations.
papers.mechanism: The onset of phase transition is linked to local variations in elemental composition and short-range ordering, which lower the effective melting onset due to kinetic and thermodynamic factors. CALPHAD predictions and observed discrepancies suggest that metastable states and microsegregation play an important role.

papers.title: Multi-principal elemental intermetallic nanoparticles synthesized via a disorder-to-order transition.
papers.system: Multi-principal element nanoparticles (e.g., PtPdAuFeCoNiCuSn quinary/octonary systems)
papers.approach: Rapid Joule heating to induce a disorder-to-order phase transition, monitored by in situ STEM and complemented with Monte Carlo modeling
papers.findings: Demonstrated that brief re-heating at ~1100 K can drive a disorder-to-order atomic rearrangement, leading to a lower Gibbs free energy configuration that is stable against further heating. The transition kinetics and ordering are highly sensitive to temperature and processing time.
papers.mechanism: The phase transition is driven by atomic diffusion that decreases the formation enthalpy (ΔHf) and stabilizes the ordered phase (ΔG_ordered < ΔG_disordered). This mechanism implicates the role of thermal energy in overcoming kinetic barriers while enabling preferential ordering at the nanoscale.

papers.title: Laser solid-phase synthesis of graphene shell-encapsulated high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
papers.system: CrMnFeCoNi HEA nanoparticles synthesized on a carbon support (LIG)
papers.approach: Laser processing with precise control of local temperature profiles and high cooling rates, combined with simulation of the spatial temperature distribution
papers.findings: Observed that laser-induced rapid heating and high local pressures induce molten bead splitting and rapid quenching, producing nanoparticles with sizes similar to those formed in lower-temperature regions despite reaching above the melting threshold.
papers.mechanism: High laser fluence creates a steep thermal gradient and transient high-pressure conditions that modify the conventional surface-tension-driven melting behavior. This leads to fragmentation of the liquid phase into small droplets that rapidly solidify, implying a strong kinetic component overriding equilibrium melting.

papers.title: Continuous synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles by in-flight alloying of elemental metals.
papers.system: In-flight alloying of elemental metal vapors (e.g., Cr, Mo, Ni, etc.) to form HEA nanoparticles in a thermal plasma jet
papers.approach: Thermal plasma processes with in-line thermofluid simulation to elucidate nucleation temperature differences and competing vapor–liquid–solid (VLS) versus vapor–solid (VS) growth mechanisms
papers.findings: Identified that the large nucleation temperature gap among elements (e.g., Mo nucleating much earlier than others) creates challenges for co-nucleation. Under certain conditions, either VLS (liquid-mediated) or VS (direct solidification) mechanisms dominate, affecting elemental homogeneity.
papers.mechanism: The interplay between partial pressures, nucleation temperatures, and the melting point depression at the nanoscale results in a competition between homogeneous mixing in the liquid state and direct vapor condensation, which governs the final phase formation.

papers.title: Kinetically-controlled laser-synthesis of colloidal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
papers.system: Colloidal HEA nanoparticles (CoCrFeMnNi) synthesized via ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation
papers.approach: Picosecond laser ablation in liquid leading to rapid cooling (estimated ~10^12 K/s) and size distribution analysis via TEM and XRD characterization
papers.findings: Demonstrated that ultrafast cooling preserves ultra-small nanoparticle sizes by kinetically quenching the structure, preventing further growth and phase segregation. Different size fractions are attributed to distinct formation mechanisms (nucleation in low-density versus molten layer instabilities).
papers.mechanism: Rapid kinetic quenching due to extremely high cooling rates suppresses grain growth and phase separation, emphasizing a non-equilibrium pathway that defines the initial phase and size distribution of HEA nanoparticles.

established: Nanoparticles exhibit depressed melting temperatures relative to bulk alloys due to size effects and altered thermal resistances.
Thermal processing (e.g., rapid heating/cooling) can trigger phase transitions such as disorder-to-order transitions.
Local compositional modulations and elemental segregation influence the onset of melting and solidification behavior in HEA systems.

approaches_tried.approach: Differential Thermal Analysis (DTA) and DSC on HEA powders
approaches_tried.outcome: Identified onset temperatures for phase transitions and melting, with reproducible events observed over multiple cycles.

approaches_tried.approach: Rapid Joule heating to induce disorder-to-order transitions
approaches_tried.outcome: Successfully generated ordered intermetallic nanoparticle phases with improved thermal stability compared to disordered phases.

approaches_tried.approach: Laser-induced heating and rapid cooling on carbon-supported precursors
approaches_tried.outcome: Achieved nanoparticles with uniform size through fragmentation of molten droplets, demonstrating a kinetic control mechanism.

approaches_tried.approach: Thermal plasma jet synthesis with in-flight alloying
approaches_tried.outcome: Revealed competing nucleation and condensation mechanisms (VLS vs VS) that affect composition uniformity.
Produced ultra-small HEA nanoparticles with controlled phase and size distribution via rapid kinetic quenching.

mechanisms: Thermodynamic-driven phase transitions influenced by Gibbs free energy differences between disordered and ordered states.
Kinetic control via rapid heating and cooling, which can suppress equilibrium growth and favor metastable phases.
Nano-size effects (e.g., melting point depression) coupled with local elemental segregation and short-range ordering.
disagreements: CALPHAD predictions sometimes do not match the experimentally observed transition temperatures, indicating complexities from nanoscale effects.
There is variability in the observed solidification paths (single-phase versus multi-phase formations) depending on the sample’s thermal history and processing method.
open_questions: What is the precise role of nanoscale elemental segregation and short-range order on the onset of melting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles?
How do controlled variations in nanoparticle size and pre-existing ordering impact the temperature range and progression of the phase transition?
To what extent do processing-induced thermal gradients and local pressure effects (e.g., from laser or plasma synthesis) alter the phase transition pathways compared to equilibrium predictions?
opportunities: Perform controlled comparisons between FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles with different size distributions (and hence different melting point depressions) under identical thermal ramp rates.
Investigate the effect of pre-synthesis ordering by comparing nanoparticles synthesized under rapid quenching versus slower cooling conditions.
Combine in situ thermal imaging with rapid thermal processing (e.g., laser or Joule heating) to correlate local temperature profiles with phase transition onset and progression.
Use complementary techniques (e.g., DTA/DSC and in situ TEM/STEM) to obtain a multi-scale understanding of the interplay between kinetic quenching and thermodynamic ordering.

directions.direction: Investigate the role of pre‐existing nanoscale elemental segregation and short‐range ordering in governing the melting onset.
directions.assessment: This approach directly ties differences in local composition and ordering to the onset of melting. Prior evidence [PMC7956699::web::004::1_introduction, PMC11427457::web::015::laser_synthesis_mechanisms] supports that elemental segregations can lower local melting points. It is feasible via controlled annealing comparisons and in situ thermal analysis.

directions.direction: Examine the influence of thermal ramp rate on disorder‐to‐order atomic rearrangements during heating.
directions.assessment: Rapid heating may kinetically arrest or delay complete melting through intermediate ordering transitions. Evidence from rapid Joule heating methods [PMC8797181::web::000::abstract] supports disorder-to-order transitions. This direction is directly testable by comparing different ramp rates under controlled conditions.

directions.direction: Study the effects of nanoparticle size and hence surface-to‐volume ratio on surface premelting phenomena.
directions.assessment: Nanoscale curvature is known to depress melting points relative to bulk. By comparing different controlled sizes, one can test whether the surface melting layer indeed governs the overall phase transition. Literature on nanoparticle melting and rapid cooling [PMC9064730::web::007::colloidal_state_of_the_laser_ablation_pr] supports the feasibility of this approach.

directions.direction: Assess the impact of local thermal gradients and transient pressure effects induced by high‐fluence laser heating on melting behavior.
directions.type: Processing (laser synthesis) and thermal gradient effects
directions.assessment: Localized high-fluence heating can produce steep thermal gradients and even transient pressure variations that modify melting behavior. Prior work [PMC11427457::web::015::laser_synthesis_mechanisms] suggests that such effects can lead to fragmentation and heterogeneous melting. The study is feasible provided careful spatial temperature mapping is employed.

candidates.hypothesis: Rapid thermal ramping induces a disorder-to-order atomic rearrangement that kinetically delays full melting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles, thus broadening the melting transition range.
candidates.intervention: Apply two distinct heating protocols: a rapid thermal ramp (e.g., 100 K/s via Joule heating) versus a slow ramp (e.g., 5 K/min), with all other parameters held constant.

candidates.hypothesis: The high surface-to-volume ratio in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles leads to preferential surface premelting driven by curvature-induced melting point depression, which then initiates overall phase transition.
candidates.intervention: Subject both small and larger nanoparticle samples to identical heating protocols (e.g., 5 K/min in inert conditions).

candidates.hypothesis: Intense, localized thermal gradients and transient high-pressure conditions from high-fluence laser heating induce heterogeneous melting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles by fragmenting molten regions and modifying conventional melting behavior.
candidates.intervention: Apply high-fluence, short-pulse laser heating with well-controlled parameters (e.g., 58.9 mJ/cm² fluence, 2000 mm/s scanning rate) and compare with samples subjected to conventional uniform furnace heating.
